title: Information Quality, Content Scope, and Audience Engagement of Popular Turkish Instagram Posts on Tooth Whitening: A Cross-Sectional Content Analysis
screen_reason: QUALITY-ONLY study. The 500 Instagram posts were scored on two rating instruments — the Descriptive Coverage Index (how many of 8 content parameters a post covers) and a Modified Treatment-Information Reliability score (DISCERN sections 2-3) — and never judged for truth or falsity against any external ground truth, so under §3 no CONTENT estimate exists. The paper does report shares of posts in the low/moderate/high bands of both instruments, which §3 says to keep as construct QUALITY, excluded from prevalence. JUDGEMENT CALL FOR THE ADJUDICATOR: §1 lists 'QUALITY-ONLY studies' as a screen-level EXCLUDE ground while §3 says the QUALITY row is 'kept, excluded from prevalence'. I followed §3 and recorded the rows as QUALITY (borderline=true) rather than screening the paper out, because that preserves the information and the rows carry no prevalence weight either way. If the project convention is to EXCLUDE quality-only papers outright, drop both rows; the paper contributes nothing to prevalence under either reading.

estimates.country: Turkey (Turkish-language posts under the Turkish hashtag #dişbeyazlatma)
estimates.measure_type: % of popular Turkish Instagram tooth-whitening posts rated LOW (0-2 of 8) on the Modified Treatment-Information Reliability score (adapted DISCERN sections 2-3)
estimates.denominator: 500 publicly accessible Turkish-language Instagram posts on tooth whitening, taken from the 'Top Posts' section of #dişbeyazlatma (676 screened, 176 excluded)
estimates.definition: Post scored 0-2 points out of 8 on the Modified Treatment-Information Reliability score (binary present/absent scoring of DISCERN sections 2 and 3), grouped as 'low' using the 0-2 / 3-5 / >=6 cutoffs carried over from prior dental social-media studies. No claim in any post was checked for accuracy against an external standard.
estimates.misinfo_def: No operational definition of misinformation is given; the concept appears only rhetorically: social media "can also disseminate inaccurate, incomplete, or commercially biased information"
estimates.page_loc: p. 11, Table 2 (B) categorical distribution; same figures in Section 3.2
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two calibrated evaluators independently scored all 500 posts after a 20-post calibration pilot; inter-rater agreement on a random 50-post (10%) subsample gave ICC = 0.988 (95% CI 0.979-0.993) for the Modified Treatment-Information Reliability score and ICC = 0.979 for the Descriptive Coverage Index; disagreements across the full sample were resolved by consensus moderated by a third senior researcher. The instruments are rating scales, not truth judgements.
estimates.moderator_quote:
Posts listed in the “Top Posts” section under this hashtag were screened, after applying predefined inclusion and
                            exclusion criteria; 500 posts were included in the final analysis.
estimates.notes: borderline=true flags the construct/screen call, not the number: the value itself is stated verbatim in Table 2(B). denom_selection=curated because Instagram's engagement-ranked 'Top Posts' section is a rank-truncated set, which the authors themselves treat as a selection-on-outcome problem. Single-issue hashtag corpus, so denom_scope=topical. population_scope=general_public because the corpus is public-facing content, but note 75.8% of posts came from dentist/clinic accounts, 14.4% from independent users and 9.8% from brand accounts. A low reliability score means the post omitted DISCERN-style elements (risks, alternatives, uncertainty), which a wholly accurate post could also do, so this is squarely QUALITY under the §3 rule.

estimates.notes: Second of the paper's two rating instruments on the same 500-post sample, so this row is not independent of the Modified Treatment-Information Reliability row (Spearman r = 0.629 between the two scores). definition_variant left false because the two instruments measure different things (coverage vs treatment-information reliability) rather than a stricter or broader version of one definition; an adjudicator who wants only one QUALITY row per paper should keep the reliability row and drop this one.

missed_or_uncertain: No prevalence-relevant estimate exists in this paper. Not extracted: (1) the source, purpose and format composition shares (dentist/clinic 75.8%, independent users 14.4%, brand 9.8%; marketing 72.0%, educational 26.0%, experience-based 2.0%; photo 47.0%, Reels 43.4%, carousel 9.6%) and the whitening-approach shares (dentist/clinic posts 55.9% in-office; independent users 45.8% DIY, 43.1% OTC) — these describe who posted and about what, not whether the content was accurate; (2) all median scores, Kruskal-Wallis tests, effect sizes, ordinal regression output, engagement rates and the r = 0.141 MTIR-engagement correlation — none is a share with a misinformation denominator; (3) the Turkish internet-penetration figures (90.9% of 16-74 year olds online, 65.4% Instagram use) cited from reference [11], excluded under R8 as figures taken from elsewhere. The paper's keyword list includes 'misinformation' and the discussion talks about 'misinformation regarding DIY whitening techniques', but no post was ever coded as false or misleading, so that framing is not backed by a measurement.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis, STROBE-reported. Sampling frame: 'Top Posts' under the Turkish hashtag #dişbeyazlatma (~316,000 posts available), browsed 1-5 November 2025 from a clean account with location and personalised recommendations disabled; 676 posts screened, 176 excluded (61 not relevant, 38 private, 27 hidden metrics, 21 non-Turkish, 18 duplicates, 11 entertainment-only), leaving 500. No response rate applies. Two calibrated evaluators scored all 500 posts independently after a 20-post pilot; ICC on a random 10% subsample was 0.979 (DCI) and 0.988 (MTIR); disagreements resolved by consensus with a third senior researcher. Acknowledged weaknesses: no a priori sample size calculation, no thematic saturation assessment, the DCI has never been psychometrically validated, and engagement served both as the sampling criterion and as an outcome (selection-on-outcome circularity).
